subjective.question: Define a bijective mapping.
subjective.answer: A mapping f : X → Y is called bijective if it is both one-to-one and onto. It is one-to-one (injective) if f(x₁) = f(x₂) implies x₁ = x₂ for all x₁, x₂ ∈ X, and it is onto (surjective) if for every y ∈ Y there exists x ∈ X with f(x) = y, i.e. f[X] = Y. A bijective mapping pairs each element of X with exactly one element of Y and vice versa, so it has an inverse mapping f⁻¹ : Y → X.

subjective.question: Define a subgroup of a group, with an example.
subjective.answer: A non-empty subset H of a group G is called a subgroup of G if H is itself a group under the same binary operation as G. It is denoted by H ≤ G. Example: (Z, +) is a subgroup of (R, +), because the integers are closed under addition, 0 ∈ Z, and the additive inverse of every integer is again an integer. Another example: {1, −1} is a subgroup of {1, −1, i, −i} under multiplication.

subjective.question: State the one-step and the two-step subgroup tests.
subjective.answer: One-step subgroup test: A non-empty subset H of a group G is a subgroup of G if and only if ab⁻¹ ∈ H for all a, b ∈ H. (For an additive group this reads: a − b ∈ H for all a, b ∈ H.) Two-step subgroup test: A subset H of a group G is a subgroup of G if and only if (i) ab ∈ H for all a, b ∈ H (closure), and (ii) b⁻¹ ∈ H for every b ∈ H (existence of inverses). Associativity is inherited from G, and taking a = b in the one-step test gives e ∈ H.

subjective.question: Define a group homomorphism and give one example.
subjective.answer: A mapping φ : (G, ·) → (H, *) is called a group homomorphism if φ(a · b) = φ(a) * φ(b) for all a, b ∈ G. Example: the function f : (Z, +) → (Zₙ, +) defined by f(x) = [x], the congruence class of x modulo n, is a homomorphism, because f(x + y) = [x + y] = [x] + [y] = f(x) + f(y). Another example is f : (R, +) → (R+, ·), f(x) = eˣ, since e^(x+y) = eˣ · eʸ.

subjective.question: Define a normal subgroup of a group.
subjective.answer: A subgroup N of a group G is called a normal subgroup of G if g⁻¹ng ∈ N for all g ∈ G and all n ∈ N. Equivalently, N is normal if and only if gN = Ng for every g ∈ G, i.e. the left and right cosets of N coincide. Every subgroup of an abelian group is normal. Example: the alternating group Aₙ is a normal subgroup of Sₙ.

subjective.question: Define the quotient group G/N of a group G by a normal subgroup N.
subjective.answer: Let N be a normal subgroup of G. The set G/N = {Ng : g ∈ G} of all cosets of N in G forms a group under the operation (Ng₁)(Ng₂) = N(g₁g₂); this operation is well defined precisely because N is normal. The group G/N is called the quotient group (or factor group) of G by N. Its identity element is the coset N itself, the inverse of Ng is Ng⁻¹, and if G is finite then |G/N| = |G| / |N|. Example: Z/nZ = Zₙ is the quotient group of (Z, +) by the subgroup nZ.

subjective.question: State the first isomorphism theorem for groups.
subjective.answer: First isomorphism theorem: Let φ : G → H be a group homomorphism with kernel K = ker φ. Then K is a normal subgroup of G and the quotient group G/K is isomorphic to the image of φ, i.e. G/ker φ ≅ Im φ, the isomorphism being given by ψ(Kg) = φ(g). In particular, if φ is onto H, then G/ker φ ≅ H.

subjective.question: Write two properties of a group homomorphism, giving a reason for each.
subjective.answer: (i) Homomorphism preserves the identity: if φ : G → G′ is a homomorphism and e, e′ are the identities of G and G′, then φ(e) = e′. Reason: φ(e) = φ(e · e) = φ(e)φ(e), and cancelling φ(e) in G′ gives φ(e) = e′. (ii) Homomorphism preserves inverses: φ(a⁻¹) = (φ(a))⁻¹ for all a ∈ G. Reason: φ(a)φ(a⁻¹) = φ(aa⁻¹) = φ(e) = e′ and similarly φ(a⁻¹)φ(a) = e′, so φ(a⁻¹) is the inverse of φ(a) in G′.

subjective.question: Show that (Z, +) is a group under addition.
subjective.answer: The integers under addition form a group: (i) Closure: the sum of two integers is an integer, so a + b ∈ Z for all a, b ∈ Z. (ii) Associativity: (a + b) + c = a + (b + c) for all a, b, c ∈ Z, since addition of integers is associative. (iii) Identity: 0 ∈ Z and a + 0 = 0 + a = a for every a ∈ Z, so 0 is the identity element. (iv) Inverses: for every a ∈ Z, −a ∈ Z and a + (−a) = 0, so every element has an inverse. Hence (Z, +) is a group. It is also abelian, since a + b = b + a.

subjective.question: Prove that (R, +) is a group.
subjective.answer: (i) Closure: the sum of two real numbers is a real number. (ii) Associativity: (a + b) + c = a + (b + c) for all real a, b, c. (iii) Identity: 0 ∈ R satisfies a + 0 = a for every a ∈ R. (iv) Inverses: for each a ∈ R, −a ∈ R and a + (−a) = 0. All four group axioms hold, so (R, +) is a group (in fact an abelian group, since addition of real numbers is commutative).

subjective.question: Prove that {1, −1, i, −i} is an abelian group under multiplication.
subjective.answer: The multiplication table of {1, −1, i, −i} is: · | 1 −1 i −i 1 | 1 −1 i −i −1 | −1 1 −i i i | i −i −1 1 −i | −i i 1 −1 Closure: every entry of the table is again in the set, so the set is closed under multiplication. Associativity is inherited from the multiplication of complex numbers. The identity is 1, since 1 · x = x for all x in the set. Inverses: 1⁻¹ = 1, (−1)⁻¹ = −1, i⁻¹ = −i, (−i)⁻¹ = i, all in the set. Hence {1, −1, i, −i} is a group under multiplication. It is abelian because the table is symmetric about the main diagonal (equivalently, multiplication of complex numbers is commutative).

subjective.question: Draw the Cayley table of the group {1, −1, i, −i} under multiplication.
subjective.answer: The Cayley (multiplication) table of the group {1, −1, i, −i} under multiplication is: · | 1 −1 i −i 1 | 1 −1 i −i −1 | −1 1 −i i i | i −i −1 1 −i | −i i 1 −1 For example, i · i = −1, i · (−i) = 1, (−1) · i = −i and (−i) · (−i) = −1.

subjective.question: Show that (S₃, ∘) is non-abelian.
subjective.answer: Take the transpositions α = (1 2) and β = (1 3) in S₃ (composition applied right to left). Then αβ : 1 → 3 → 3, 3 → 1 → 2, 2 → 2 → 1, so αβ = (1 3 2). And βα : 1 → 2 → 2, 2 → 1 → 3, 3 → 3 → 1, so βα = (1 2 3). Since αβ = (1 3 2) ≠ (1 2 3) = βα, composition in S₃ is not commutative. Hence (S₃, ∘) is a non-abelian group.

subjective.question: Write two groups that are abelian.
subjective.answer: (Z, +) is abelian because addition of integers is commutative: a + b = b + a for all a, b ∈ Z. (Q, +) is abelian for the same reason: the sum of two rational numbers does not depend on the order of the terms. (Other correct examples: (R, +), (Zₙ, +), and the Klein four-group.)

subjective.question: Prove that every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic.
subjective.answer: Let G = ⟨a⟩ be cyclic and H ≤ G. If H = {e} there is nothing to prove. Otherwise H contains some aᵏ with k ≠ 0; replacing k by −k if needed, H contains a positive power of a. Let m be the least positive integer such that aᵐ ∈ H. We claim H = ⟨aᵐ⟩. Let aᵗ ∈ H. Divide t by m: t = qm + r with 0 ≤ r < m. Then aʳ = aᵗ (aᵐ)^(−q) ∈ H, since aᵗ ∈ H and aᵐ ∈ H. By the minimality of m, r = 0, so aᵗ = (aᵐ)ᵠ ∈ ⟨aᵐ⟩. Thus H = ⟨aᵐ⟩, which is cyclic. Hence every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic.

subjective.question: Suppose G = ⟨a⟩ with |a| = 30. Find |a²¹| and ⟨a²¹⟩.
subjective.answer: |a²¹| = |a| / gcd(|a|, 21) = 30 / gcd(30, 21) = 30 / 3 = 10. And ⟨a²¹⟩ = ⟨a^gcd(30, 21)⟩ = ⟨a³⟩, the (unique) subgroup of G of order 10.

subjective.question: Write the identity permutation of (S₄, ∘).
subjective.answer: The identity permutation of (S₄, ∘) is the identity mapping e : {1, 2, 3, 4} → {1, 2, 3, 4}, e(i) = i for all i, written in two-row notation as e = ( 1 2 3 4 ; 1 2 3 4 ). It satisfies e ∘ p = p ∘ e = p for every permutation p of S₄. (In the same way, the identity permutation of D₄ and D₅ is the identity mapping — geometrically the rotation through 0°.)

subjective.question: Write the elements of the dihedral group D₄.
subjective.answer: The dihedral group D₄ is the group of symmetries of a square. It has 8 elements: the four rotations e (through 0°), r (through 90°), r² (through 180°) and r³ (through 270°), and the four reflections s, sr, sr² and sr³ (reflections in the two diagonals and in the two midlines of the square). Thus D₄ = {e, r, r², r³, s, sr, sr², sr³}, with r⁴ = e, s² = e and srs = r⁻¹. It is also called the octic group.

subjective.question: Find all the orbits of the permutation α = ( 1 2 3 4 5 ; 5 4 2 1 3 ).
subjective.answer: Compute the images: α(1) = 5, α(5) = 3, α(3) = 2, α(2) = 4, α(4) = 1. Starting from 1 we get 1 → 5 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 1, which already passes through every element of {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}. Hence α has only one orbit, namely {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} itself, and α is the single cycle (1 5 3 2 4).

subjective.question: Let p be a permutation of a set S. Prove that the relation a ~ b if and only if b = pⁿ(a) for some n ∈ Z is an equivalence relation.
subjective.answer: Reflexive: for every a, a = p⁰(a), so a ~ a. Symmetric: if a ~ b, then b = pⁿ(a) for some n ∈ Z, so a = p⁻ⁿ(b), giving b ~ a. Transitive: if a ~ b and b ~ c, then b = pᵐ(a) and c = pⁿ(b) for some m, n ∈ Z, so c = pⁿ(pᵐ(a)) = p^(m+n)(a), giving a ~ c. The relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, hence an equivalence relation. (Its equivalence classes are the orbits of p.)

subjective.question: Is (R, +) cyclic? If yes, write its generators.
subjective.answer: No, (R, +) is not cyclic. If it were generated by a single element a, then every real number would be an integer multiple of a, i.e. R = {na : n ∈ Z}. For a = 0 this gives only {0}, and for a ≠ 0 the element a/2 ∈ R is not an integer multiple of a — a contradiction. Hence (R, +) has no generator at all: it has no cyclic generator, neither 1 nor any other real number.

subjective.question: Write the right cosets of 3Z in Z.
subjective.answer: The cosets of 3Z in Z are obtained by adding a representative of each remainder class modulo 3: 0 + 3Z = 3Z = {..., −3, 0, 3, 6, ...}, 1 + 3Z = {..., −2, 1, 4, 7, ...} and 2 + 3Z = {..., −1, 2, 5, 8, ...}. These are all the (right, and equally left) cosets of 3Z in Z; there are exactly 3 of them, so the index [Z : 3Z] = 3.

subjective.question: Let H be a subgroup of a group G and a, b ∈ G. Prove that |aH| = |bH|.
subjective.answer: Define a map φ : aH → bH by φ(ah) = bh for h ∈ H. It is well defined and one-to-one: if ah₁ = ah₂ then h₁ = h₂ by cancellation in G, so bh₁ = bh₂, and conversely φ(ah₁) = φ(ah₂) implies bh₁ = bh₂, hence h₁ = h₂. It is onto, since every element of bH has the form bh = φ(ah). Thus φ is a bijection between aH and bH, so |aH| = |bH|. (In fact every coset of H has exactly |H| elements.)

subjective.question: Let N be a normal subgroup of a group G. Prove that gN = Ng for all g ∈ G.
subjective.answer: Since N is normal, by definition gNg⁻¹ = N for every g ∈ G (equivalently gng⁻¹ ∈ N for all n ∈ N). Multiplying on the right by g gives gN = Ng for every g ∈ G. Hence the left coset gN and the right coset Ng of N are equal for every g ∈ G, which is exactly the statement gN = Ng.

subjective.question: State Lagrange's theorem and write two of its properties (consequences).
subjective.answer: Lagrange's theorem: If G is a finite group and H is a subgroup of G, then the order of H divides the order of G, i.e. |H| divides |G|, and the quotient |G| / |H| is the index of H in G. Two consequences (properties): (i) The order of every element of G divides the order of G, because the order of an element equals the order of the cyclic subgroup it generates. (ii) Every group of prime order is cyclic — such a group has no proper nontrivial subgroups, so any non-identity element generates it. (Another consequence: a^|G| = e for every a ∈ G.)

subjective.question: Let f : (R, +) → (R+, ·) be defined by f(x) = eˣ. Prove that f is an isomorphism.
subjective.answer: First, f is a homomorphism: for x, y ∈ R, f(x + y) = e^(x+y) = eˣ · eʸ = f(x) f(y). Second, f is one-to-one: if f(x) = eˣ = 1 = e⁰ then x = 0, so ker f = {0}, which shows f is injective. Third, f is onto R+: for any y > 0, taking x = ln y gives f(x) = e^(ln y) = y. Being a bijective homomorphism, f is an isomorphism of (R, +) onto (R+, ·), with inverse the logarithm function g(y) = ln y.

subjective.question: Find all the abelian groups of order 360 up to isomorphism.
subjective.answer: By the fundamental theorem of finite abelian groups, the number of abelian groups of order 360 (up to isomorphism) is p(3) · p(2) · p(1) = 3 · 2 · 1 = 6, since 360 = 2³ · 3² · 5¹ and the numbers of partitions of 3, 2, 1 are 3, 2, 1. The six groups are: Z₈ × Z₉ × Z₅; Z₈ × (Z₃ × Z₃) × Z₅; (Z₄ × Z₂) × Z₉ × Z₅; (Z₄ × Z₂) × (Z₃ × Z₃) × Z₅; (Z₂ × Z₂ × Z₂) × Z₉ × Z₅; (Z₂ × Z₂ × Z₂) × (Z₃ × Z₃) × Z₅. The first of these is the cyclic group Z₃₆₀.
